title: Your name day
hook: the feast of your patron saint
tomorrow: what does a feast day actually taste like?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: your first birthday, the baptism date sitting in a parish book. Today, the name that was spoken over the water.
screen: `YOUR FIRST BIRTHDAY.` → `THE NAME OVER THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Scroll any list of popular baby names: Luna, Nova, River. Not one is on the Church's calendar of saints. A name day is the feast of the saint who shares your name. So what happens when nobody does? One aunt says every child needs a saint. A cousin says her daughter's name is holy enough already. Ask two Catholics and you may get two answers, each with a real reason behind it.
screen: `LUNA, NOVA, RIVER.` → `NOT ON THE CALENDAR.` → `TWO ANSWERS, TWO REASONS.`

segments.voice: The first side says: give the child a saint. The old Code of Canon Law, from 1917, told the priest to see that a child received a Christian name, and if the parents wouldn't choose one, to add a saint's name in the register himself. Their case is friendship. A saint's name hands a child a companion in heaven and a feast that's hers from the start. In some families the name day is the bigger party, el santo, with the birthday a quieter second. The second side says: the name can be new. The current code, from 1983, asks only that parents, godparents and pastor avoid a name foreign to Christian sense. Their case: holiness isn't a closed list. Every saint's name was once nobody's, and a child named River could be the first holy one to carry it. Some choose a patron later anyway. Both sides stand on the same ground. The Catechism says God calls each one by name, and quotes Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have called thee by thy name: thou art mine." One to tell a friend: Revelation promises a white stone with a new name on it, known only to the one who receives it.
screen: `GIVE THE CHILD A SAINT.` · `A COMPANION AND A FEAST.` · `THE NAME CAN BE NEW.` · `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.` · then, large: `YOUR SAINT'S DAY.`

segments.voice: Make a small plan. Which saint's day is yours, or which saint would you choose? Pick the date, one person to invite, and one food to share. If you pray, you can ask that saint to pray for you; otherwise, just let the plan take shape.
Your name day. The feast of the saint whose name you carry, or the patron you've chosen for yourself. Today's word.
Hold on to this: your saint's day, a feast with a friend's name on it. That's today.

howItsDone: In some Catholic families a person's name day, the feast of their patron saint, is celebrated with Mass, a meal or a small gift; Catholics may also choose a patron saint, often at confirmation.

chat.says: is there even a saint sofia? abuela says yes. mia says just pick a saint i like. who's right?
options: Both work: find a Sofia on the calendar, or choose a patron. That day is yours.
Abuela. If no saint has your exact name, you don't get a name day.
Mia, sort of. Name days are just birthdays with a different date.
chat.meaning: A name day is the feast of the saint you're named for or have chosen. Both sides agree God calls each one by name.
